Almost Optimal Multiple Source Shortest Paths and Reachability **Abstract** Given a graph, computing distances and reachabilities from a small set of vertices to the whole graph is an important primitive both in theory and in practice. In this paper, we study this problem in various important settings. In undirected unweighted graphs, while computing single-source shortest path (SSSP) requires _O(n_2) time in dense graphs, all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) can be computed in \(\hat{O}(n^\omega)=O(n^{2.372})\) time [Seidel ’95] providing significant savings over running _n_ SSSP instances separately. However, if one needs to compute multiple-source shortest paths (MSSP) from a set of \(n^\sigma\) vertices, the previously best known running time was \(\hat{O}(min\{n^\omega,n^{2+\sigma}\})\): either by running APSP or running SSSP from each of the \(n^\sigma\) sources. On the other hand, a standard reduction shows that computing MSSP from \(n^\sigma\) sources is at least as hard as computing the Boolean matrix product between an \(n^\sigma\times n\) matrix and an \(n\times n\) matrix. This lower bound has a gap from the state-of-the-art algorithm and therefore, MSSP can potentially be solved much faster. The first main result of our paper is an algorithm for MSSP on undirected unweighted graphs that matches this lower bound. In particular, using fast rectangular matrix multiplication, our algorithm runs in \(\hat{O}(n^{\omega(\sigma,1,1)})\) time, which gives a smooth interpolation between the SSSP algorithm and the APSP algorithm. We also extend our algorithm to the case where the graph has small integer weights. The main technical tool behind our first main result is a novel graph decomposition, which may be of independent interest. As applications, we improve the state-of-the-art running times for hop-sets construction and computing +4-distance emulators. Next, we study the multiple-source reachability problem, where we need to determine whether a given set of \(n^\sigma\) vertices can reach each of the vertices in a given directed graph. Multiple-source reachability can also be solved in \(\hat{O}(min\{n^\omega,n^{2+\sigma}\})\) time, and similarly is as hard as computing Boolean matrix product between an \(n^\sigma\times n\) matrix and an \(n\times n\) matrix. [Elkin and Trehan ’24, ’25] gave the first nontrivial algorithm for multiple-source reachability that runs in \(\hat{O}(n^{1+2\omega(\sigma,1,1)/3})\) time. This only beats the trivial \(\hat{O}(min\{n^\omega,n^{2+\sigma}\})\) time for a restricted range of \(\sigma\). We significantly improve their results, by giving an algorithm that runs in \(\hat{O}(n^{\omega(\sigma,1,1)})\) time, again matching the running time for Boolean matrix product. Our algorithm for multiple-source reachability can be generalized to MSSP on DAGs with small integer weights. As an application, we provide an _O(n_2.084) time algorithm for computing an \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)-size shortcut set that reduces diameter to _O(n_1/3), improving the previous \(\widetilde{O}(n^{7/3})\) time algorithm [Kogan and Parter ’22, ’23]. ∗Supported by NSF HDR TRIPODS Phase II grant 2217058 (EnCORE Institute). ## 1 Introduction

Computing shortest paths is among the most fundamental problems in computer science. Many of its variants have been studied in the literature, and the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem is one of the most fundamental variants and has been extensively studied.

In APSP, one needs to compute the distance between every pair of nodes in a given _n_-vertex graph.<sup>1</sup> One could run Dijkstra’s algorithm _n_ times to obtain an _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) running time. An alternative classical algorithm, the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, also achieves an _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) running time. A long series of works (e.g. \[Fre76, Dob90, Tak92, Tak98, Han04, Pet04, Zwi04, Cha05, Han06, Cha10, HT12\]) improved poly-logarithmic factors over the classic _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) running time, culminating in the current fastest algorithm by Williams \[Wil18\] with \(n^3/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})}\) running time for general weighted graphs, a super poly-logarithmic improvement over the classic _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) running time. Due to the lack of polynomial improvements, the APSP hypothesis, stating that there is no \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) time algorithm for any \(\varepsilon>0\) that computes APSP for _n_-node graphs, is among the most popular hypotheses in Fine-Grained Complexity.

Faster algorithms are known in unweighted graphs. If the graph is undirected, Seidel \[Sei95\] gave an algorithm computing APSP in \(\widehat{O}(n^\omega)\) time.<sup>2</sup> More generally, on undirected graphs with positive integer weights bounded by _B_, APSP can be computed in \(\widehat{O}(Bn^\omega)\) time \[SZ99, AGM97\]. For directed unweighted graphs, the current fastest algorithm was designed by Zwick \[Zwi02\], which runs in _O(n_<sup>2.528</sup>) time.

A simpler version of distance problems is reachability problems, where one needs to decide whether a vertex can reach another vertex. All-Pairs Reachability, also popularly known as transitive closure, is another fundamental problem in graph algorithms. It is known to be equivalent to the Boolean Matrix Multiplication problem, and can be solved in \(\widehat{O}(n^\omega)\) time \[FM71, Mun71\].

Computing all the pairwise distances (resp. reachability) gives full distance (resp. reachability) information of the graph, but it also comes with a cost: it is computationally expensive. In contrast, computing the distance between a fixed pair of vertices only takes near-linear time in all the variants mentioned above, though it gives much less information than APSP. A natural question is to study the intermediate cases:

**Question 1.** _Can we compute some distances faster than all distances?_

Graphs arising in theory and practice applications often contain a small set of hot spots, where distances between these hot spots and other vertices are more likely to be queried. For instance, in the network connecting all locations in a city, distances from places like grocery stores, shopping malls and parks are more likely to be queried than distances between two residential buildings. In theory, many applications using distance computations only need distances from a fixed small set of vertices to other vertices (e.g. approximate APSP \[DHZ96, DKR<sup>+</sup>22, SY24, DFK<sup>+</sup>24, JKSV26\], approximate diameter \[RV13, CLR<sup>+</sup>14, CGR16\] and shortcut sets and hopsets \[UY91\]).

Motivated by these applications, we study the multiple source version of distance and reachability problems. More formally, we study:

**Definition 1.1** (Multiple Source Shortest Paths / Reachability)**.** _Given graph G_=(_V,E_) _and a set of sources_ \(S_\mathrm{in}\subseteq V\) _, compute_ dist(_s,v_) _for all_ \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\) _and_ \(v\in V\) _. In the reachability version of the problem, we only need to determine if the distance is_ \(\infty\) _or not._

### 1.1 Shortest Paths in Undirected Unweighted Graphs

Our first result is for Multiple-Source Shortest Paths in undirected unweighted graphs. There are two straightforward algorithms to solve MSSP: we can either solve SSSP for every \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\), or solve APSP. For undirected graphs, there were no other known algorithms besides these two approaches, to the best of our knowledge. This leads to the following question that motivated our work, instantiating a specific instance of Question 1.

<sup>1</sup>Throughout this paper, we consider dense graphs with _m=O(n_<sup>2</sup>). <sup>2</sup>\(\omega\le 2.372\) \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\] is the fast matrix multiplication exponent, or the smallest constant _c_ such that an \(n\times n\times n\) matrix product can be computed in _n_<sup>_c+o_(1)</sup> time. \(\widehat{O}\) hides sub-polynomial factors.

_Is there an_ MSSP _algorithm faster than_ \(\widehat{O}(min(|S_\mathrm{in}|m,n^\omega))\)?

We answer this question in the affirmative, giving the first algorithm that beats this running time. In fact, our algorithm is essentially optimal, by tying the running time of our algorithm to Boolean matrix multiplication.

**Theorem 1.2.** MSSP _on undirected unweighted graphs is equivalent to_ BMM(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n), up to n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> _factors, for randomized algorithms._<sup>3</sup> _In particular, there is a randomized algorithm computing_ MSSP _on undirected, unweighted graphs in n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>T<sub>BMM</sub>(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n_) _time._

Here, BMM(_a,b,c_) denotes Boolean matrix product instances between \(a\times b\) matrices and \(b\times c\) matrices, and T<sub>BMM</sub>(_a,b,c_) denotes the running time of such instances. In particular, T<sub>BMM</sub>(_a,b,c_) can be upper bounded by the running time for computing products of general \(a\times b\) and \(b\times c\) matrices, utilizing fast matrix multiplication algorithms (see Figure 1 for an illustration of the quantitative improvements we achieve). The reduction from Boolean matrix multiplication to MSSP in the above theorem can be achieved with standard approaches.<sup>4</sup> We also extend our algorithm to handle graphs with small integer weights.

**Theorem 1.3.** MSSP _on undirected graphs with integer edge weights in_ \[_B_\] _is equivalent to_ MPP(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n|B), up to n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>log_B factors, for randomized algorithms._<sup>5</sup> _In particular, if_ \(B\le\mathrm{poly}(n)\)_, there is a randomized algorithm computing_ MSSP _on undirected graphs with integer edge weights in_ \[_B_\] _in n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>T<sub>MPP</sub>(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n|B_) _time._

Here, MPP(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n|B_) denotes Min-Plus product between an \(|S_\mathrm{in}|\times n\) matrix and an \(n\times n\) matrix, whose entries are from \([B]\cup\{\infty\}\), and T<sub>MPP</sub>(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n|B_) denotes the running time of such instances. It is known that \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(a,b,c|B)=\widetilde{O}\left(B\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(a,b,c)\right)\) \[AGM97\].

Our algorithms give a smooth interpolation between the SSSP algorithm and the APSP algorithms \[Sei95\] and \[SZ99\]. When _s=n_, our algorithm serves as an alternative algorithm for APSP in undirected graphs with unit or small integer weights (See \[CVX21\] for another alternative algorithm).

The key technical ingredient of our algorithms is a novel low diameter decomposition, which may be of independent interest. We define the notion of a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition. We say \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) is a \((d,\phi)\)-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition if (1) \(\mathrm{diam}(G[V_i])\le d\) for all _i_, and (2) \(\sum_i|N(V_i)|\le\phi n\). While the first condition is reminiscent of standard low diameter decompositions, the second condition is different: instead of requiring that the number of edges between clusters is small (see e.g. \[BNW22\]), our decomposition requires that the neighborhoods of the clusters are small. In particular, while there may be many edges incident to any given cluster, we ensure that they do not expand and hit too many distinct vertices. Note that our bound on the neighborhood size is global rather than local, there may be clusters where \(|N(V_i)|>\phi|V_i|\), but the sum of the neighborhoods is at most \(\phi n\). We show how to obtain an (_n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>_,n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>)-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition in _n_<sup>2+_o_(1)</sup> time.

**Theorem 1.4.** _There is a randomized n_<sup>2+_o_(1)</sup> _time algorithm that computes a_ \(\left(2^{O\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n}\right)},2^{O\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n}\right)}\right)\)_-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition._

We also give some natural applications of our MSSP algorithm. We obtain improvements over the state- of-the-art algorithms with simple reductions, establishing the practical impact of the MSSP problem (see Section 5.3 for formal statements).

<sup>3</sup>Our equivalence holds under the mild assumption that \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(2m,2n,2n)\ge 4\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(m,n,n)\) for all \(m,n\ge 1\). Note that this assumption essentially requires that BMM scales at least linearly with input size. We remark that our improved running time holds regardless of the assumption. See proof of Claim 5.8 for details. <sup>4</sup>Let _A_ be an \(s\times n\) matrix and _B_ an \(n\times n\) matrix. We build a three layered graph with vertex layers _V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>_,V_<sub>3</sub>, where |_V_<sub>1</sub>|=_s_, |_V_<sub>2</sub>|=|_V_<sub>3</sub>|=_n_, encode _A_ into \(V_1\times V_2\) (i.e., there is an edge if the corresponding entry of _A_ is 1, and no edge otherwise) and _B_ into \(V_2\times V_3\), and note that for \(i\in V_1,j\in V_3\), dist(_i,j_)=2 if and only if (_AB_)\[_i,j_\]=1. <sup>5</sup>Like Theorem 1.2, the equivalence holds under the mild assumption that \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(2m,2n,2n|B)\ge 4\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(m,n,n|B)\) for all \(m,n\ge 1\). As before, our improved running time holds regardless of the assumption.

#### Hop-sets.

A (weighted) set of edges _F_ is a \(\beta\)-hop-set for graph _G_=(_V,E_) if every pair of vertices (_u,v_) in \(H=(V,E\cup F)\) has the same distance as in _G_ and there exists a shortest path of at most \(\beta\) hops. Research in hop-sets (and the related concept of shortcut sets) aims to minimize both the size of the hop-set (ideally linear) and the hop diameter \(\beta\). A folklore sampling algorithm produces \(\beta\)-hop-sets of size \(n^2/\beta^2\): sample a set _S_ of \(n/\beta\) vertices, and add all edges between \((u,v)\in S\times S\) with weight dist(_u,v_). In particular, we may obtain an \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{1/2}\right)\)-hop-set of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n\right)\). Bodwin and Hoppenworth showed that the folklore sampling is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors: any exact hop-set of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n\right)\) must have \(\beta=\widetilde{\Omega}\left(n^{1/2}\right)\) \[BH23\].

However, the sampling algorithm does not compute a hop-set efficiently, since previous algorithms for computing all distances between \(S\times S\) for _S_ of size \(\sqrt{n}\) require time \(\widetilde{O}(min(n^{2.5},n^\omega))=O(n^{2.372})\). Our improved MSSP algorithm allows us to compute all \(S\times S\) distances in time \(n^{\omega(0.5,1,1)}=O(n^{2.043})\) \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\].<sup>6</sup>

#### Distance Emulators.

Emulators are sparse graphs that faithfully preserve the distances of a graph. Formally, given a graph _G_=(_V,E_), a (possibly weighted) set of edges _F_ is a +_k_-emulator if \(dist_G(u,v)\le dist_{(V,F)}(u,v)\le dist_G(u,v)+k\) for all pairs of vertices _u,v_. Emulators (and related constructions such as graph spanners) have been the subject of intense study since their introduction \[PS89\], and have been useful objects with many applications, including compact routing schemes \[PU89, CW00, Cow01, TZ01, RTZ08\], distance oracles \[TZ05, BK06\], and broadcasting \[FPZW04\].

Several constructions of additive emulators are known: +2-emulators of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{3/2}\right)\) \[ACIM99\], +4- emulators of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{4/3}\right)\) \[DHZ00\], and +6-emulators of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{4/3}\right)\) \[BKMP05\]. We remark that both the +2 and +6 constructions are spanners (_F_ is a subset of _E_). However, the sparsest +4-spanner known has size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{7/5}\right)\) \[Che13\]. Furthermore, it is known that no emulator (or any data structure) of size \(n^{4/3-\Omega(1)}\) can achieve error _k=n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> \[AB17\]. Thus, significant effort has been devoted to characterizing the additive error of emulators of linear size \[TZ06, BV15, HP21, EGN23, KP23b, Hop24, HJVX24\].

Both the +2 and +6-emulators can be constructed in near-linear time \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^2\right)\) \[DHZ00, Woo10\]. However, the best known algorithm for constructing the +4-emulator requires time \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^{7/3}\right)\) \[DHZ00\]. With our MSSP algorithm, we obtain a construction in time \(\widehat{O}(n^{\omega(2/3,1,1)})=O(n^{2.1321})\) \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\].

## 1.2 Reachability in Directed Graphs

In the Multiple-Source Reachability problem, the goal is to determine whether _s_ can reach _v_ for every pair \((s,v)\in S_\mathrm{in}\times V\) . As all-pairs reachability can be solved in \(\widehat{O}(n^\omega)\) time \[FM71, Mun71\], and single-source reachability can be solved in _O(m_) time, Multiple-Source Reachability can be solved in \(\widehat{O}(min(|S_\mathrm{in}|m,n^\omega))\) time, similar to MSSP on undirected unweighted graphs. Standard reduction from BMM(_S_<sub>in</sub>_,n,n_) also works for Multiple-Source Reachability, establishing an \(\Omega(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(S_\mathrm{in},n,n))\) lower bound.

Recently, Elkin and Trehan \[ET24, ET25\] gave an alternative algorithm for Multiple-Source Reachability. Their algorithm runs in \(\widehat{O}\left(n\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(S_\mathrm{in},n,n)^{2/3}\right)\), which beats \(\widehat{O}(min(S_\mathrm{in}m,n^\omega))\) for certain values of |_S_<sub>in</sub>|, but unfortunately never meets the \(\Omega(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(S_\mathrm{in},n,n))\) lower bound (see Figure 1).

In our second main result, we design an algorithm for Multiple-Source Reachability that matches the \(\Omega(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(S_\mathrm{in},n,n))\) lower bound.

**Theorem 1.5.** _Multiple Source Reachability is equivalent to_ BMM(|_S_<sub>in</sub>|_,n,n), up to_ polylog(_n_) _factors. In particular, there is a deterministic algorithm computing Multiple-Source Reachability in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}\left(|S_\mathrm{in}|,n,n\right)\right)\) _time._

## 1.3 Shortest Paths in Directed Acyclic Unweighted Graphs

Finally, we study MSSP on directed unweighted graphs, whose running time landscapes seem to be more complicated. Consider APSP as an example. APSP for undirected unweighted graphs runs in \(\widehat{O}(n^\omega)\) time \[Sei95\], while APSP for directed unweighted graphs runs in \(\widehat{O}(n^{2+\mu})\) time \[Zwi02\], where \(\mu\le 0.528\) \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\] is the solution to \(\omega(1,\mu,1)=2+\mu\). As we can see, even representing the running time requires more effort in the directed case.

One can rephrase the running time of Zwick’s algorithm as<tbc>

\(\widetilde{O}\left(\mathrm{max}_{1\le t\le n}\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(n,t,n|n/t)\right),\)

\(\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\mathrm{max}_{1\le t\le n}\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(n,n/t,n|t)\right).\)

## Shortcut Sets

A set of edges _F_ is a _D_-shortcut-set for graph _G_=(_V,E_) if \(H=\left(V,E\cup F\right)\) has the same transitive closure as _G_ and \(\mathrm{diam}(G\cup F)\le D\). For a directed graph, \(\mathrm{diam}(G)=\mathrm{max}_{\left(u,v\right)\in\mathrm{TC}\left(G\right)}\mathrm{dist}\left(u,v\right)\) is the maximum distance between any two vertices for \(\left(u,v\right)\in\mathrm{TC}\left(G\right)\), where TC(_G_) is the transitive closure of _G_. Shortcut sets have applications in reachability and shortest paths computation in many settings \[KS97, HKN14, HKN15, FN18, LJS19, Fin20, GW20, BGW20\]. Similar to exact hop-sets, a folklore sampling algorithm yields a shortcut set of diameter \(O(\sqrt{n})\) and size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n\right)\). A breakthrough result of Kogan and Parter \[KP22b\] showed that in fact there exist shortcut sets of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n\right)\) and diameter _O(n_<sup>1/3</sup>), while no linear size shortcut set can achieve diameter _o(n_<sup>1/4</sup>) \[BH23, VXX24\]. As with hop-sets, known algorithms for computing shortcut sets are not optimal, with the current best algorithm computing diameter _D_-shortcut- sets of size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^2/D^3+n\right)\) in time \(\widetilde{O}\left(mn/D^2\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(n^3/D^2\right)\) whenever \(D=O(\sqrt{n})\) \[KP23a\] (\[KP22a\]’s running time is the same for dense graphs). As an application of Theorem 1.6, we compute shortcut-sets in dense graphs of diameter _D_ and size \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^2/D^3+n\right)\) in time \(\widetilde{O}\left(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}\left(n/D^2,n,n|D,1\right)\right)\) (see Theorem 6.6). Our algorithm is faster than \[KP23a\] for all values of \(D=O(\sqrt{n})\), as illustrated in Figure 2. For the important case _D=n_<sup>1/3</sup>, our running time is _O(n_<sup>2.064</sup>).

### 1.4 Related Works

Question 1 is a long-term research paradigm that has been approached from many angles:

1. Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP): The most classical and successful example \[Dij59, FT87\], SSSP computes a set of _n_ distances from _s_.<tbc>

2. Extremal distances: The diameter, radius, and eccentricities are well-studied problems in distance computation, resulting in both approximation algorithms \[RV13, CLR<sup>+</sup>14, BRS<sup>+</sup>18, CGR16\] and hardness results \[RV13, Bon22, DLV25\].<tbc>

3. _n_-Pairs Shortest Paths (NPSP): Given _n_ pre-specified pairs of vertices (_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>i</sub>_), compute dist(_s<sub>i</sub>,t<sub>i</sub>_) for all _i_. In contrast to SSSP, the NPSP problem computes _n_ arbitrary pre-specified distances. The study of NPSP was initiated by \[ACIM99\], with several recent works reigniting interest in the question \[DJVW22, CHL25\].<tbc>

4. Distance Oracles: Preprocess _G_ so that given any query (_u,v_), return dist(_u,v_) efficiently. Distance oracles capture the setting where we do _not_ know what distances are interesting in advance. A long line of work has established a variety of approximation algorithms \[Tho04, TZ05, PR10, Che14, CDW17, CGMW19, CZ22\] and hardness results \[ABKZ22, JX23, ABF23\].

### 1.5 Open Questions

We conclude the introduction with some open questions.

1. We establish an equivalence between BMM and MSSP on unweighted, undirected graphs. Can a similar equivalence (with some other matrix product) be established for MSSP on directed graphs? Concretely, can Theorem 1.6 be generalized to compute shortest paths on directed graphs (not necessarily DAGs)?<tbc>

2. In our work, we have shown that a \((d,\phi)\)-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition can be computed efficiently, where \(d,\phi=n^{o(1)}\). In principle, it may be possible to obtain a decomposition where |_N(V<sub>i</sub>_)|=_O_(|_V<sub>i</sub>_|) and diam(_V<sub>i</sub>_)=_O_(log_n_) for all _V<sub>i</sub>_. Can we obtain such a decomposition, and do so efficiently? Even the weaker setting where \(d,\phi=\text{polylog}(n)\) would be interesting.<tbc>

3. Our decomposition algorithm runs in _n_<sup>2+_o_(1)</sup> time, which is efficient for dense graphs, but is inefficient on sparse graphs. Can we compute a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition in _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time? Are there other applications of low diameter small neighborhood decompositions?<tbc>

4. Currently, our algorithm for computing MSSP is randomized, since our algorithm for computing our low diameter small neighborhood decomposition requires randomness. Can we derandomize our low diameter small neighborhood decomposition algorithm?<tbc>

5. We use MSSP to develop faster algorithms for hop-set, shortcut-set, and distance emulator constructions. It would be interesting to find further applications of an efficient MSSP algorithm.

## 2 Technical Overview

We give an overview of our techniques. Recall that our goal is to design an MSSP algorithm that performs better than the naive \(\widetilde{O}\left(min(|S_\text{in}|n^2,n^{\omega+o(1)})\right)\) time obtained by either running SSSP from every source or computing APSP. ## 2.1 Warm-Up: A Simple Improvement

## 2.2 Optimal Multiple-Source Shortest Paths

The above algorithm suggests a potential more generic approach: when we try to grow the BFS tree of some source by one layer, we could wait until many sources need to do so, and group the computation into a matrix multiplication. To further improve the running time, it is natural to use more thresholds, instead of a single threshold _T_. Now when we group multiple sources together, we need a better bound on the size of the union of the corresponding layers. In order to really take advantage of batch processing, we need these layers to have large overlaps - if all the layers are disjoint, then batch processing does not help at all. In the above simple improvement, we only perform batch processing for very large layers, and we simply used _n_ as the upper bound on the size of the union. For smaller layers, why wouldn’t layers of different sources be mostly disjoint (like random sets)? Hence, in order to proceed, we develop some structural insights of undirected unweighted graphs, in particular, a novel low diameter decomposition.

Typically, low diameter decompositions require the number of edges between clusters to be small (see e.g. \[BNW22\]). For our application however, we will utilize something different: the sum of the size of the neighborhoods of each cluster is almost linear (i.e. _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>).<sup>8</sup> Formally, we develop a decomposition \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) of the vertices satisfying:

1. diam(_V<sub>i</sub>_)=_n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> for all _i_.<tbc>

2. \(\sum_i|N(V_i)|=n^{1+o(1)}\).

Before describing how to obtain such a decomposition (see Theorem 4.2), let us see how it is useful. Recall that we use level(_s_) to index the most recently computed layer of the shortest path tree rooted at _s_. Now, instead of computing _L(s,_level(_s_)+1) from _L(s,_level(_s_)) by considering all pairs of vertices, we compute \(L(s,\text{level}(s)+1)\cap N(V_i)\) from \(L(s,\text{level}(s))\cap V_i\) for all _i_ where \(V_i\cap L(s,\text{level}(s))\neq\emptyset\). Note that correctness follows from the fact that \(\{V_i\}_{i=1}^k\) cover _L(s,_level(_s_)) so that \(\{N(V_i)\}_{i=1}^k\) cover _L(s,_level(_s_)+1).

Since we do not consider _L(s,_level(_s_)) all at once, we need to keep track of which vertices in the layer whose neighborhoods we have already examined. Let A(_s_) denote the vertices in _L(s,_level(_s_)) which we still need to examine, called the active vertices. Note that A(_s_) is initialized to _L(s,_level(_s_)) and each iteration of the while loop removes some _V<sub>i</sub>_ from A(_s_).

We say _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to _s_ if \(V_i\cap\mathcal{A}(s)\neq\emptyset\). For each cluster _V<sub>i</sub>_, denote score(_i_) the number of sources _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to. We say a cluster _V<sub>i</sub>_ is _ready_ when \(\text{score}(i)\ge\frac{|S_\text{in}||N(V_i)|}{n^{1+o(1)}}\) . Observe that there is always one ready cluster. If not, by the second property of our decomposition, we have \(\sum_i\text{score}(i)<|S_\text{in}|\). However, since there is at least one cluster relevant to each source, we obtain a contradiction via \(\sum\text{score}(i)\ge|S_\text{in}|\).

We now describe our improved algorithm (see Theorem 5.1 for full algorithm).

Correctness follows from our discussion above. We proceed to analyze the running time, where we will bound the time required by all iterations of the while loop where _V<sub>i</sub>_ is chosen as the ready cluster.

First, we claim that for any fixed source _s_, _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to _s_ for _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> iterations (see Lemma 5.5). This follows from the first property of our decomposition \((\text{diam}(V_i)\le n^{o(1)})\) so that _V<sub>i</sub>_ can intersect at most _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> distinct layers of the shortest path tree of _s_. The result follows from observing that _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to _s_ for one iteration per layer of the shortest path tree (i.e. one value of level(_s_)).

Second, we claim that _V<sub>i</sub>_ is selected as a ready cluster in \(\frac{n^{1+o(1)}}{|N(V_i)|}\) iterations (see Lemma 5.6). Let _T(i_) denote all iterations where _V<sub>i</sub>_ is selected. Let \(S'(t)\) denote the set of sources _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to in iteration \(t\in T(i)\). Then, over all iterations where _V<sub>i</sub>_ is selected, we have \(\sum_t|S'(t)|=|S_\text{in}|n^{o(1)}\). On the other hand, since _V<sub>i</sub>_ is ready, \(\text{score}(i)=|S'(t)|\ge\frac{|S_\text{in}||N(V_i)|}{n}\) . Thus, we have \(|T(i)|\le\frac{n^{1+o(1)}}{|N(V_i)|}\) .

We now bound the time required by all iterations where _V<sub>i</sub>_ is selected, breaking our analysis into two cases: small clusters and large clusters. ## 2.3 Low Diameter Small Neighborhood Decomposition

We now describe how to efficiently obtain a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition (Theorem 4.2). We say \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) is a \((d,\phi)\)-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition (LDSND) if \(\mathrm{max}_i\mathrm{diam}(V_i)\le d\) and \(\sum_i|N(V_i)|\le\phi n\) (see Definition 4.1).

Consider the following algorithm for obtaining a single low diameter cluster. Pick an arbitrary vertex _v_ and let \(N(v,r):=\{u\in V:\mathrm{dist}(v,u)\le r\}\) denote the _r_-neighborhood of _v_. We claim \(|N(v,3^k)|\le\phi^k\) for some \(k\le\lceil\mathrm{log}_\phi n\rceil\). Otherwise \(|N(v,3^{\lceil\mathrm{log}_\phi n\rceil})|>n\) becomes a contradiction (see Figure 3). Setting \(\phi=2^{O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})}\), we get that \(k\le O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})\) and \(3^k\le 2^{O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})}\) so that _N(v,_3_<sup>k</sup>_) has small diameter.

Motivated by this observation, our decomposition C will consist of balls _N(v,_3_<sup>k</sup>_) for some _v_ and _k_. For each \(0\le k\le\mathrm{log}_\phi n\), we sample \(S_k\subseteq V\) by including each vertex with probability \(p_k\sim\phi^{-k}\). Then, for each \(u\in S_k\), we add _N(u,_3_<sup>k</sup>_) to C if \(|N(u,3^k+1)|\le\phi^{k+1}\). Since \(|S_k|=O(n\phi^{-k})\) with high probability, the total time required is at most \(O(\sum_k|S_k|\phi^{2k+2})=O(\sum_kn\phi^{k+2})=n^{2+o(1)}\).

Above, we have argued that each set has small diameter. Furthermore, since \(|S_k|=O(n\phi^{-k})\) with high probability, we have that \(\sum_{u\in S_k}|N(u,3^k+1)|=O(n\phi)=n^{1+o(1)}\), as desired.

It remains to argue that every vertex \(v\in N(u,3^k)\) for some \(N(u,3^k)\in\mathcal{C}\). Let \(k\ge 1\) be the smallest positive integer satisfying \(|N(v,3^k)|\le\phi^k\) so that \(|N(v,3^{k-1})|>\phi^{k-1}\). Note that such a _k_ always exists since |_N(v,_1)|_\>_1 unless _v_ is an isolated vertex. Then, with high probability, some \(u\in S_{k-1}\) hits _N(v,_3<sup>_k_-1</sup>). Then, since \(\mathrm{dist}(u,v)\le 3^{k-1}\) and \(2\cdot 3^{k-1}+1\le 3^k\), we have \(|N(u,3^{k-1}+1)|\le|N(v,2\cdot 3^{k-1}+1)|\le|N(v,3^k)|\le\phi^k\) , resulting in _N(u,_3<sup>_k_-1</sup>) being added to C, as desired.

Note that the above process gives a covering of the vertices. We can obtain a decomposition by removing duplicated vertices from the clusters.

## 2.4 Extension to Bounded Weights

Finally, we describe how to extend the algorithm to handle weighted graphs with small integer weights bounded by _B_. Note that an algorithm that computes MSSP on graphs with integer weights bounded by \(\Theta(B)\) also computes the rectangular (min,+)-product of two integer matrices with entries bounded by _B_. Given \(S_\mathrm{in}\times n\) matrix _X_ and \(n\times n\) matrix _Y_ , construct a three-layer graph with _V_<sub>1</sub>=_S_<sub>in</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>=\[_n_\]_,V_<sub>3</sub>=\[_n_\] and edges (_s,u_) for \(s\in V_1,u\in V_2\) with weight 10_B+X_\[_s,u_\] and edges (_u,v_) for \(u\in V_2,v\in V_3\) with weight 10_B+Y_\[_u,v_\]. Then, dist(_s,v_)=20_B_+(_X⋆Y_)\[_s,v_\] whenever \((X\star Y)[s,v]<\infty\) and is at least 40_B_ otherwise.

Thus, our goal is to develop an algorithm that runs in \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(|S_\mathrm{in}|,n,n|B)=\widetilde{O}\left(B\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(|S_\mathrm{in}|,n,n)\right)\) time, where \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(n^a,n^b,n^c|B)\) denotes the time required to compute the (min,+)-product between integer matrices of dimension \(n^a\times n^b\times n^c\) with integer entries bounded by _B_.

We first describe an \(\hat{O}(B^2\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(|S_\mathrm{in}|,n,n))\) time algorithm. Treat _G_ as an unweighted graph, and compute an (_n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>_,n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>)-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition.

Now, fix a source _s_. To ensure correctness, in order to compute _L(s,_level(_s_)+1) we need two modifications to account for the fact that edge weights can be up to _B_. We need to (1) consider any cluster _V<sub>i</sub>_ that intersects _L(s,r_) for any \(\mathrm{level}(s)-B\unknown r\unknown\mathrm{level}(s)\), and (2) compute \(N(V_i)\cap L(s,\mathrm{level}(s)+1)\) via a _B_- bounded (min,+)-product. Revisiting the analysis of our unweighted algorithm, we obtain a running time of \(\hat{O}(B^2\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(|S_\mathrm{in}|,n,n))\) since (1) implies that _V<sub>i</sub>_ is relevant to _s_ for _Bn_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> iterations (in contrast to _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>), while (2) implies that we must use _B_-bounded (min,+)-products in place of a Boolean product.

To ensure that each cluster is relevant to any source _s_ only for _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> iterations of the while loop, we instead take the following approach. Consider graphs _G<sub>b</sub>_ for \(b\unknown\mathrm{log}B\) consisting of all edges with weight between 2_<sup>b</sup>_ and 2<sup>_b_+1</sup>. We obtain low diameter small neighborhood decompositions for all _G<sub>b</sub>_ as unweighted graphs, denoted \(\mathcal{C}_b=\left\{V_i^{(b)}\right\}\). Now, while each cluster \(V_i^{(b)}\) has diameter 2_<sup>b</sup>n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>, we only need to consider cluster edges in _G<sub>b</sub>_ incident to \(V_i^{(b)}\) for every 2_<sup>b</sup>_ layers of the shortest path tree from _s_, since each of these edges has weight at least 2_<sup>b</sup>_. Our final algorithm for bounded weights selects a cluster that is relevant to many sources, and relaxes all edges of the appropriate weight range incident to this cluster. To ensure correctness and efficiency, we carefully manage which vertices are active for each source and edge weight class, ensuring that the shortest path tree of each source is built accurately (see Theorem 1.3 for details).

## 2.5 Multiple Source Reachability

Our algorithm for Multiple Source Reachability (and MSSP on DAGs) employs a simple recursive scheme. Assume that _G_ is sorted in topological order. Let \(\mathrm{pred}(\pi,v)\) denote the predecessor of _v_ in path \(\pi\). For any interval \[_L,R_\] of \(\ell\) vertices, we employ a recursive scheme `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>_,L,R_) with the following input/output conditions:

Input: reach(_s,v_) is computed if there is a path \(\pi\) from \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\) to \(v\unknown R\) where \(\mathrm{pred}(\pi,v)\unknown L\).

Output: reach(_s,v_) is computed for all \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\) and \(v\unknown R\).

Our Multiple Source Reachability algorithm computes `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>,0,|_V_|). In this overview, we describe how to compute `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>_,L,R_). Let _M_=(_L+R)/_2 be the midpoint of the interval. Note that we can compute `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>_,L,M_) since the input condition is satisfied. Our goal is to satisfy the input condition of `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>_,M,R_) which would satisfy the output condition of `complete`(_G,S_<sub>in</sub>_,L,R_). To do so, we need to ensure reach(_s,v_) is computed for any path \(\pi\) from _s_ to _v_ with \(L\unknown\mathrm{pred}(\pi,v)\unknown M\). We can do this with a single computation of BMM by constructing matrix _X_ as a \(S_\mathrm{in}\times[L,M]\) containing reach(_s,u_) for \(u\in[L,M]\) and a matrix _Y_ as a \([L,M]\times[M,R]\) submatrix of the adjacency matrix, ensuring that all paths passing through \[_L,M_\] are accounted for. The running time of the recursion is thus

\(T(\ell)=2T(\ell/2)+\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(S_\mathrm{in},\ell,\ell)\)

which yields \(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(S_\mathrm{in},n,n)\) by appealing to the root-heavy case of the Master Theorem. Our algorithm for MSSP on DAGs employs a similar recursive structure, replacing each BMM instance with an appropriate Min-Plus Product.

## 4 Low Diameter Small Neighborhood Decomposition

In this section, we present an efficient algorithm for computing a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition. We begin by defining the desired properties.

**Definition 4.1.** _A partition of V into subsets V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub> is a_ \((d,\phi)\)_-low diameter small neighborhood decomposition_ (LDSND_) of G_=(_V,E_) _if:_

1. _(Low Diameter)_ \(\mathrm{diam}_G(V_i)\le d\) _for all_ \(i\in[k]\).<tbc>

_2._ _(Total Neighborhood Size)_ \(\sum_{i=1}^k|N(V_i)|\le\phi n\).

We now give an efficient algorithm for computing a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition.

**Theorem 4.2.** _For any_ \(\psi>1\)_, there is a randomized_ \(O\left(n^2\psi^4\mathrm{log}n\mathrm{log}_\psi n\right)\) _time algorithm that given an n-vertex m-edge undirected, unweighted graph G computes a_ \((d,\phi)\)-LDSND _where_ \(d=6\cdot 3^{\mathrm{log}_\psi n}\) _and_ \(\phi=O\left(\psi\mathrm{log}n\mathrm{log}_\psi n\right)\) _Furthermore, this algorithm computes N(V<sub>i</sub>_) _for all subsets V<sub>i</sub> in the decomposition._

_Proof._ We give an algorithm that computes a collection of subsets _V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>k</sub>_ such that \((1)V=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_k\), \((2)\mathrm{diam}_G(V_i)\le d\) for all _i_, and \((3)\sum_i|N(V_i)|\le\phi n\). From here, it is easy to observe that by removing duplicate vertices, we obtain a partition that is a \((d,\phi)\)-LDSND, as removing vertices can only reduce the diameter and the total neighborhood size.

First, we show that any vertex _v_ has a small-diameter neighborhood that does not expand.

**Claim 4.3.** _For every_ \(v\in V\)_, there exists_ \(0\le k<\lceil\mathrm{log}_\psi n\rceil\) _such that_ \(|N(v,3^{k+1})|\le\psi^{k+1}\) _and_ \(|N(v,3^k)|>\psi^k\).

_Proof._ Observe that \(|N(v,3^0)|=|N(v,1)|\ge 2>\psi^0\) (recall we assume the graph is connected). Also, \(|N(v,3^{\lceil log_\psi n\rceil})|=n\le\psi^{\lceil log_\psi n\rceil}\). The claim thus follows. We now argue that an appropriate collection of _N(v,_3_k_) suffice to provide a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition of _G_. Consider the following procedure. 1. Let \(\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\emptyset\),\(\mathcal{N}\leftarrow\emptyset\). 2. For \(0\le k<\lceil log_\psi n\rceil\): (a) Sample a random subset \(S_k\subseteq V\) by including each \(u\in V\) with probability \(p_k=min\left(1,\frac{3logn}{\psi^k}\right)\). (b) For each \(u\in S_k\): i. Compute _N(u,_3_k_+1) using BFS. ii. If \(|N(u,3^k+1)|\le\psi^{k+1}\): update \(\mathcal{C}\leftarrow^\sqcup\left\{N(u,3^k)\right\}\) and \(\mathcal{N}\leftarrow^\sqcup\left\{N(u,3^k+1)\right\}\).
(Whenever \(|N(u,3^k+1)|>\psi^{k+1}\), we terminate the invocation of BFS early.) 3. Return C,N. We claim that our algorithm returns a low diameter small neighborhood decomposition. We begin with the first property. Let \(v\in V\) . Let _k_ be an arbitrary integer guaranteed by Claim 4.3. We claim that _Sk_ contains a vertex in _N(v,_3_k_) with high probability. The claim holds trivially whenever _pk_=1 (i.e. _Sk=V_). For _pk\<_1, since \(|N(v,3^k)|>\psi^k\), \(Pr(N(v,3^k)\cap S_k=\emptyset)\le(1-p_k)^{\psi^k}2. Towards the second property, we bound the diameter of each set _N(u,_3_k_) with \(k\le\lceil log_\psi n\rceil\) by \(2\left(3^k\right)\le 2\cdot 3^{\lceil log_\psi n\rceil}\le 6\cdot 3^{log_\psi n}.\) Towards the third property, we can bound the size of all _N(Vi_)=_N(u,_3_k_+1) by \(\sum_k|S_k|\psi^{k+1}\). Using a standard Chernoff bound, we can conclude with high probability that all \(|S_k|=O\left(\frac{nlogn}{\psi^k}\right)\). ## Correctness.

We argue that our algorithm terminates and outputs correct distances. As before, we can show that the estimated distances are always valid.

**Lemma 5.10.** _In every iteration of the while loop_ \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)\ge\mathrm{dist}(s,v)\) _for all_ \(s\in S_\mathrm{in},v\in V\) .

_Proof of Lemma 5.10._ We argue that at the end of each iteration of the while loop \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)\) can be realized by a path in _G_ from _s_ to _v_ for all \(s\in S_\mathrm{in},v\in V\) . Consider the first iteration where this is not the case.

Then, during this iteration, \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)\) was updated, i.e. we update \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)\leftarrow\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,u)+\mathrm{wt}(u,v)<\mathrm{dist}(s,v)\) for some \(u\in\mathcal{A}(s,b)\cap V_i^{(b)}\) with \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)=\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,u)+\mathrm{wt}(u,v)\). Note that \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,u)\) was computed in some previous iteration. Thus, there is a path from _s_ to _u_ with length \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,u)\), which we may extend to _v_ via the edge (_u,v_) with weight wt(_u,v_). This is a contradiction.

The remainder of the proof is dedicated to showing that our algorithm produces exact shortest distances. We begin with some useful claims about level(_s,b_), level(_s_), whose proofs are deferred.

**Claim 5.11.** _In any iteration of the while loop,_ level(_s_) _increases by at most one for all_ \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\).

**Claim 5.12.** _Let_ \(s\in S_\mathrm{in}\) _and_ \(\ell\le\mathrm{ccc}(s)\)_. Then, for every b such that_ \(\ell\) _is a multiple of b, there exists an iteration where_ \(\mathrm{level}(s)=\mathrm{level}(s,b)=\ell\) _at the beginning of the iteration._

Next, we prove that our algorithm iteratively computes correct distances, analogously to Lemma 5.3.

**Lemma 5.13.** _At the end of each iteration of the while loop,_ \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,v)=\mathrm{dist}(s,v)\) _for all_ \(\mathrm{dist}(s,v)\le\mathrm{level}(s)\)_. In particular, for all_ \(r\le\mathrm{level}(s)\), \(L(s,r)=\hat{L}(s,r)\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction, where the base case follows identically as Lemma 5.3. Now, let \(\ell>0\). Consider the first iteration of the while loop where \(\mathrm{level}(s)=\ell\). In this iteration, we incremented level(_s_). By Claim 5.11, level(_s_) increments by at most 1, so that at the end of the previous iteration, we have \(\mathrm{level}(s)=\ell-1\).

By induction, we have \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,u)=\mathrm{dist}(s,u)\) for all \(\mathrm{dist}(s,u)<\ell\). Consider a vertex with \(\mathrm{dist}(s,v)=\ell\) and a shortest path _s=w_<sub>0</sub>_,...,w_<sub>_p_-1</sub>_,w<sub>p</sub>=v_ where \(\mathrm{dist}(s,w_{p-1})<\ell\). Suppose \((w_{p-1},v)\in E_b\) and \(w_{p-1}\in V_i^{(b)}\). By induction, \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(s,w_{p-1})=\mathrm{dist}(s,w_{p-1})\) and \(w_{p-1}\in\hat{L}(s,r)\) for \(r=\mathrm{dist}(s,w_{p-1})\ge\ell-2b+1\) since edge weights in _E<sub>b</sub>_ are less than 2_b_. ### 5.3.1 Hop-Set Construction

Our first application is the first non-trivial algorithm for explicitly constructing hop-sets.

**Definition 5.22.** _A set of weighted edges F is a_ \(\beta\)_-hop-set for G_=(_V,E,_wt) _if_ \(\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)=\mathrm{dist}_{G\cup F}(u,v)\) _for all_ \(u,v\in V\) _and for every u,v, there is a path_ \(\pi\) _of at most_ \(\beta\) _hops from u to v such that_ \(\pi\) _is a shortest path between u,v._

We give an efficient algorithm for computing exact \(\beta\)-hop-sets on dense graphs, improving upon the known \(\mathrm{min}\left(n^3/\beta,n^\omega\right)\) time algorithm.

**Theorem 5.23.** _For all_ \(\beta\ge 1\)_, there is a randomized_ \(Bn^{o(1)}\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MUL}(n/\beta,n,n)\) _time algorithm that computes a_ \(\beta\)_-hop-set with_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^2/\beta^2\right)\) _edges on undirected graphs with integer weights in_ \[_B_\].

_Proof._ When \(\beta\le 30\mathrm{log}n\), we observe that the theorem is true by computing APSP in _Bn_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>T<sub>MUL</sub>(_n,n,n_) time and adding edges of weight dist(_u,v_) between every pair of vertices. Thus, we assume \(\beta>30\mathrm{log}n\). Consider the following algorithm.

1. **Input:** Undirected graph _G_ with integer weights in \[_B_\].<tbc>

2. Sample \(S\subseteq V\) by including each vertex independently with probability \(\frac{30\mathrm{log}n}{\beta}\)<tbc>

3. Compute \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(S,V)\leftarrow\mathrm{MSSP}(G,S)\).<tbc>

4. Compute \(F\leftarrow\{(a,b)\text{s.t.}a,b\in S\}\) where edge (_a,b_) has weight \(\widehat{\mathrm{d}}(a,b)\).<tbc>

5. **Output:** Weighted edge set _F_.

First, we argue that _F_ is a \(\beta\)-hop-set. Consider a shortest path of at least \(\beta/3\) nodes. Then, the probability that none of these nodes is included in _S_ is at most

\(\left(1-\frac{30\mathrm{log}n}{\beta}\right)^{\beta/3}\le n^{-10}\)

so that union bounding over _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) shortest paths, we can ensure with high probability that all shortest paths of at least \(\beta/3\) nodes include one node in _S_. Then, for any shortest path of length \(\ell\ge\beta\), \(\pi=v_0,\dots,v_{\beta/3},\dots,v_{\ell-\beta/3},\dots,v_\ell\), we have \(v_i,v_j\in S\) for \(i\le\beta/3\) and \(j\ge\ell-\beta/3\). Then, adding _F_, we have<tbc>

the path \(\pi'=v_0,\dots,v_i,v_j,\dots,v_\ell\) of hop length at most \(2\beta/3+1\). Furthermore, \(\text{wt}(v_i,v_j)=\widehat{\text{d}}(v_i,v_j)=\text{dist}(v_i,v_j)\) by correctness of the MSSP algorithm.

\(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{MPP}(n_1,n_2,n_3|B_1,B_2)=O\left(\mathsf{T}_\mathrm{BMM}(n_1B_1,n_2,n_3B_2)\right)\)

<tbc>_and if B=B_<sub>1</sub>+_B_<sub>2</sub>,
